CHAPTER XLII

Letters of fire on the church wall had just inquired, with an appearance
of genuine curiosity, why there was no mass for the duke in this time of
trouble. The supernatural expostulation had been seen by many, and had
gradually faded, leaving the spectators glued there gaping. The upshot
was, that the corporation, not choosing to be behind the angelic powers
in loyalty to a temporal sovereign, invested freely in masses. By this
an old friend of ours, the cure, profited in hard cash; for which he had
a very pretty taste. But for this I would not of course have detained
you over so trite an occurrence as a miracle.


Denys begged for his arms. “Why disgrace him as well as break his
heart?”

“Then swear on the cross of thy sword not to leave the bastard's service
until the sedition shall be put down.” He yielded to necessity, and
delivered three volleys of oaths, and recovered his arms and liberty.

The troops halted at “The Three Fish,” and Marion at sight of him cried
out, “I'm out of luck; who would have thought to see you again?” Then
seeing he was sad, and rather hurt than amused at this blunt jest, she
asked him what was amiss? He told her. She took a bright view of the
case. Gerard was too handsome and well-behaved to come to harm. The
women too would always be on his side. Moreover, it was clear that
things must either go well or ill with him. In the former case he would
strike in with some good company going to Rome; in the latter he would
return home, perhaps be there before his friend; “for you have a trifle
of fighting to do in Flanders by all accounts.” She then brought him
his gold pieces, and steadily refused to accept one, though he urged her
again and again. Denys was somewhat convinced by her argument, because
she concurred with his own wishes, and was also cheered a little by
finding her so honest. It made him think a little better of that world
in which his poor little friend was walking alone.

Foot soldiers in small bodies down to twos and threes were already on
the road, making lazily towards Flanders, many of them penniless, but
passed from town to town by the bailiffs, with orders for food and
lodging on the innkeepers.

Anthony of Burgundy overtook numbers of these, and gathered them under
his standard, so that he entered Flanders at the head of six hundred
men. On crossing the frontier he was met by his brother Baldwyn, with
men, arms, and provisions; he organized his whole force and marched on
in battle array through several towns, not only without impediment,
but with great acclamations. This loyalty called forth comments not
altogether gracious.

“This rebellion of ours is a bite,” growled a soldier called Simon, who
had elected himself Denys's comrade.

Denys said nothing, but made a little vow to St. Mars to shoot this
Anthony of Burgundy dead, should the rebellion, that had cost him
Gerard, prove no rebellion.

That afternoon they came in sight of a strongly fortified town; and a
whisper went through the little army that this was a disaffected place.

But when they came in sight, the great gate stood open, and the towers
that flanked it on each side were manned with a single sentinel
apiece. So the advancing force somewhat broke their array and marched
carelessly.

When they were within a furlong, the drawbridge across the moat rose
slowly and creaking till it stood vertical against the fort and the
very moment it settled into this warlike attitude, down rattled the
portcullis at the gate, and the towers and curtains bristled with lances
and crossbows.

A stern hum ran through the bastard's front rank and spread to the rear.

“Halt!” cried he. The word went down the line, and they halted. “Herald
to the gate!” A pursuivant spurred out of the ranks, and halting twenty
yards from the gate, raised his bugle with his herald's flag hanging
down round it, and blew a summons. A tall figure in brazen armour
appeared over the gate. A few fiery words passed between him and the
herald, which were not audible, but their import clear, for the herald
blew a single keen and threatening note at the walls, and came galloping
back with war in his face. The bastard moved out of the line to meet
him, and their heads had not been together two seconds ere he turned in
his saddle and shouted, “Pioneers, to the van!” and in a moment hedges
were levelled, and the force took the field and encamped just out of
shot from the walls; and away went mounted officers flying south, east,
and west, to the friendly towns, for catapults, palisades, mantelets,
raw hides, tar-barrels, carpenters, provisions, and all the materials
for a siege.

The bright perspective mightily cheered one drooping soldier. At
the first clang of the portcullis his eyes brightened and his temple
flushed; and when the herald came back with battle in his eye he saw it
in a moment, and for the first time this many days cried, “Courage, tout
le monde, le diable est mort.”

If that great warrior heard, how he must have grinned!

The besiegers encamped a furlong from the walls, and made roads; kept
their pikemen in camp ready for an assault when practicable; and sent
forward their sappers, pioneers, catapultiers, and crossbowmen. These
opened a siege by filling the moat, and mining, or breaching the wall,
etc. And as much of their work had to be done under close fire of
arrows, quarels, bolts, stones, and little rocks, the above artists “had
need of a hundred eyes,” and acted in concert with a vigilance, and an
amount of individual intelligence, daring, and skill, that made a siege
very interesting, and even amusing: to lookers on.

The first thing they did was to advance their carpenters behind rolling
mantelets, to erect a stockade high and strong on the very edge of the
moat. Some lives were lost at this, but not many; for a strong force of
crossbowmen, including Denys, rolled their mantelets up and shot over
the workmen's heads at every besieged who showed his nose, and at every
loophole, arrow-slit, or other aperture, which commanded the particular
spot the carpenters happened to be upon. Covered by their condensed
fire, these soon raised a high palisade between them and the ordinary
missiles from the pierced masonry.

But the besieged expected this, and ran out at night their boards or
wooden penthouses on the top of the curtains. The curtains were built
with square holes near the top to receive the beams that supported these
structures, the true defence of mediaeval forts, from which the besieged
delivered their missiles with far more freedom and variety of range
than they could shoot through the oblique but immovable loopholes of the
curtain, or even through the sloping crenelets of the higher towers.
On this the besiegers brought up mangonels, and set them hurling
huge stones at these woodworks and battering them to pieces.
Contemporaneously they built a triangular wooden tower as high as the
curtain, and kept it ready for use, and just out of shot.

This was a terrible sight to the besieged. These wooden towers had taken
many a town. They began to mine underneath that part of the moat the
tower stood frowning at; and made other preparations to give it a warm
reception. The besiegers also mined, but at another part, their object
being to get under the square barbican and throw it down. All this time
Denys was behind his mantelet with another arbalestrier, protecting the
workmen and making some excellent shots. These ended by earning him
the esteem of an unseen archer, who every now and then sent a winged
compliment quivering into his mantelet. One came and struck within an
inch of the narrow slit through which Denys was squinting at the moment.
“Peste,” cried he, “you shoot well, my friend. Come forth and receive my
congratulations! Shall merit such as thine hide its head? Comrade, it
is one of those cursed Englishmen, with his half ell shaft. I'll not die
till I've had a shot at London wall.”

On the side of the besieged was a figure that soon attracted great
notice by promenading under fire. It was a tall knight, clad in complete
brass, and carrying a light but prodigiously long lance, with which he
directed the movements of the besieged. And when any disaster befell the
besiegers, this tall knight and his long lance were pretty sure to be
concerned in it.

My young reader will say, “Why did not Denys shoot him?” Denys did shoot
him; every day of his life; other arbalestriers shot him; archers shot
him. Everybody shot him. He was there to be shot, apparently. But the
abomination was, he did not mind being shot. Nay, worse, he got at last
so demoralised as not to seem to know when he was shot. He walked his
battlements under fire, as some stout skipper paces his deck in a
suit of Flushing, calmly oblivious of the April drops that fall on his
woollen armour. At last the besiegers got spiteful, and would not waste
any more good steel on him; but cursed him and his impervious coat of
mail.

He took those missiles like the rest.


Gunpowder has spoiled war. War was always detrimental to the solid
interests of mankind. But in old times it was good for something: it
painted well, sang divinely, furnished Iliads. But invisible butchery,
under a pall of smoke a furlong thick, who is any the better for that?
Poet with his note-book may repeat, “Suave etiam belli certamina magna
tueri;” but the sentiment is hollow and savours of cuckoo. You can't
tueri anything but a horrid row. He didn't say, “Suave etiam ingentem
caliginem tueri per campos instructam.”

They managed better in the Middle Ages.

This siege was a small affair; but, such as it was, a writer or minstrel
could see it, and turn an honest penny by singing it; so far then the
sport was reasonable, and served an end.

It was a bright day, clear, but not quite frosty. The efforts of the
besieging force were concentrated against a space of about two hundred
and fifty yards, containing two curtains and two towers, one of which
was the square barbican, the other had a pointed roof that was built
to overlap, resting on a stone machicolade, and by this means a row of
dangerous crenelets between the roof and the masonry grinned down at the
nearer assailants, and looked not very unlike the grinders of a modern
frigate with each port nearly closed. The curtains were overlapped with
penthouses somewhat shattered by the mangonels, trebuchets, and other
slinging engines of the besiegers. On the besiegers' edge of the moat
was what seemed at first sight a gigantic arsenal, longer than it was
broad, peopled by human ants, and full of busy, honest industry,
and displaying all the various mechanical science of the age in full
operation. Here the lever at work, there the winch and pulley, here the
balance, there the capstan. Everywhere heaps of stones, and piles of
fascines, mantelets, and rows of fire-barrels. Mantelets rolling, the
hammer tapping all day, horses and carts in endless succession rattling
up with materials. Only, on looking closer into the hive of industry,
you might observe that arrows were constantly flying to and fro, that
the cranes did not tenderly deposit their masses of stone, but flung
them with an indifference to property, though on scientific principles,
and that among the tubs full of arrows, and the tar-barrels and the
beams, the fagots, and other utensils, here and there a workman or a
soldier lay flatter than is usual in limited naps, and something more
or less feathered stuck in them, and blood, and other essentials, oozed
out.

At the edge of the moat opposite the wooden tower, a strong penthouse,
which they called “a cat,” might be seen stealing towards the curtain,
and gradually filling up the moat with fascines and rubbish, which the
workmen flung out at its mouth. It was advanced by two sets of ropes
passing round pulleys, and each worked by a windlass at some distance
from the cat. The knight burnt the first cat by flinging blazing
tar-barrels on it. So the besiegers made the roof of this one very
steep, and covered it with raw hides, and the tar-barrels could not harm
it. Then the knight made signs with his spear, and a little trebuchet
behind the walls began dropping stones just clear of the wall into the
moat, and at last they got the range, and a stone went clean through the
roof of the cat, and made an ugly hole.

Baldwyn of Burgundy saw this, and losing his temper, ordered the great
catapult that was battering the wood-work of the curtain opposite it to
be turned and levelled slantwise at this invulnerable knight. Denys and
his Englishman went to dinner. These two worthies being eternally on
the watch for one another had made a sort of distant acquaintance, and
conversed by signs, especially on a topic that in peace or war maintains
the same importance. Sometimes Denys would put a piece of bread on the
top of his mantelet, and then the archer would hang something of the
kind out by a string; or the order of invitation would be reversed.
Anyway, they always managed to dine together.

And now the engineers proceeded to the unusual step of slinging
fifty-pound stones at an individual.

This catapult was a scientific, simple, and beautiful engine, and very
effective in vertical fire at the short ranges of the period.

Imagine a fir-tree cut down, and set to turn round a horizontal axis on
lofty uprights, but not in equilibrio; three-fourths of the tree being
on the hither side. At the shorter and thicker end of the tree was
fastened a weight of half a ton. This butt end just before the discharge
pointed towards the enemy. By means of a powerful winch the long
tapering portion of the tree was forced down to the very ground, and
fastened by a bolt; and the stone placed in a sling attached to the
tree's nose. But this process of course raised the butt end with its
huge weight high in the air, and kept it there struggling in vain
to come down. The bolt was now drawn; Gravity, an institution which
flourished even then, resumed its sway, the short end swung furiously
down, the long end went as furiously round up, and at its highest
elevation flung the huge stone out of the sling with a tremendous jerk.
In this case the huge mass so flung missed the knight; but came down
near him on the penthouse, and went through it like paper, making an
awful gap in roof and floor. Through the latter fell out two inanimate
objects, the stone itself and the mangled body of a besieger it had
struck. They fell down the high curtain side, down, down, and struck
almost together the sullen waters of the moat, which closed bubbling
on them, and kept both the stone and the bone two hundred years, till
cannon mocked those oft perturbed waters, and civilization dried them.

“Aha! a good shot,” cried Baldwyn of Burgundy.

The tall knight retired. The besiegers hooted him.

He reappeared on the platform of the barbican, his helmet being just
visible above the parapet. He seemed very busy, and soon an enormous
Turkish catapult made its appearance on the platform and aided by the
elevation at which it was planted, flung a twentypound stone some two
hundred and forty yards in the air; it bounded after that, and knocked
some dirt into the Lord Anthony's eye, and made him swear. The next
stone struck a horse that was bringing up a sheaf of arrows in a cart,
bowled the horse over dead like a rabbit, and spilt the cart. It was
then turned at the besiegers' wooden tower, supposed to be out of shot.
Sir Turk slung stones cut with sharp edges on purpose, and struck it
repeatedly, and broke it in several places. The besiegers turned two
of their slinging engines on this monster, and kept constantly slinging
smaller stones on to the platform of the barbican, and killed two of
the engineers. But the Turk disdained to retort. He flung a forty-pound
stone on to the besiegers' great catapult, and hitting it in the
neighbourhood of the axis, knocked the whole structure to pieces, and
sent the engineers skipping and yelling.

In the afternoon, as Simon was running back to his mantelet from a
palisade where he had been shooting at the besieged, Denys, peeping
through his slit, saw the poor fellow suddenly stare and hold out his
arms, then roll on his face, and a feathered arrow protruded from his
back. The archer showed himself a moment to enjoy his skill. It was the
Englishman. Denys, already prepared, shot his bolt, and the murderous
archer staggered away wounded. But poor Simon never moved. His wars were
over.

“I am unlucky in my comrades,” said Denys.

The next morning an unwelcome sight greeted the besieged. The cat was
covered with mattresses and raw hides, and fast filling up the moat. The
knight stoned it, but in vain; flung burning tar-barrels on it, but in
vain. Then with his own hands he let down by a rope a bag of burning
sulphur and pitch, and stunk them out. But Baldwyn, armed like a
lobster, ran, and bounding on the roof, cut the string, and the work
went on. Then the knight sent fresh engineers into the mine, and
undermined the place and underpinned it with beams, and covered the
beams thickly with grease and tar.

At break of day the moat was filled, and the wooden tower began to move
on its wheels towards a part of the curtain on which two catapults
were already playing to breach the hoards, and clear the way. There was
something awful and magical in its approach without visible agency, for
it was driven by internal rollers worked by leverage. On the top was a
platform, where stood the first assailing party protected in front by
the drawbridge of the turret, which stood vertical till lowered on to
the wall; but better protected by full suits of armour. The beseiged
slung at the tower, and struck it often, but in vain. It was well
defended with mattresses and hides, and presently was at the edge of the
moat. The knight bade fire the mine underneath it.

Then the Turkish engine flung a stone of half a hundredweight right
amongst the knights, and carried two away with it off the tower on to
the plain. One lay and writhed: the other neither moved nor spake.

And now the besieging catapults flung blazing tar-barrels, and fired the
hoards on both sides, and the assailants ran up the ladders behind the
tower, and lowered the drawbridge on to the battered curtain, while the
catapults in concert flung tar-barrels and fired the adjoining works
to dislodge the defenders. The armed men on the platform sprang on the
bridge, led by Baldwyn. The invulnerable knight and his men-at-arms met
them, and a fearful combat ensued, in which many a figure was seen
to fall headlong down off the narrow bridge. But fresh besiegers kept
swarming up behind the tower, and the besieged were driven off the
bridge.

Another minute, and the town was taken; but so well had the firing of
the mine been timed, that just at this instant the underpinners gave
way, and the tower suddenly sank away from the walls, tearing the
drawbridge clear and pouring the soldiers off it against the masonry,
and on to the dry moat. The besieged uttered a fierce shout, and in a
moment surrounded Baldwyn and his fellows; but strange to say, offered
them quarter. While a party disarmed and disposed of these, others fired
the turret in fifty places with a sort of hand grenades. At this work
who so busy as the tall knight. He put the fire-bags on his long spear,
and thrust them into the doomed structure late so terrible. To do this
he was obliged to stand on a projecting beam of the shattered hoard,
holding on by the hand of a pikeman to steady himself. This provoked
Denys; he ran out from his mantelet, hoping to escape notice in the
confusion, and levelling his crossbow missed the knight clean, but sent
his bolt into the brain of the pikeman, and the tall knight fell heavily
from the wall, lance and all. Denys gazed wonder-struck; and in that
unlucky moment, suddenly he felt his arm hot, then cold, and there was
an English arrow skewering it.

This episode was unnoticed in a much greater matter. The knight, his
armour glittering in the morning sun, fell headlong, but turning as he
neared the water, struck it with a slap that sounded a mile off.

None ever thought to see him again. But he fell at the edge of the
fascines on which the turret stood all cocked on one side, and his spear
stuck into them under water, and by a mighty effort he got to the side,
but could not get out. Anthony sent a dozen knights with a white flag to
take him prisoner. He submitted like a lamb, but said nothing.

He was taken to Anthony's tent.

That worthy laughed at first at the sight of his muddy armour, but
presently, frowning, said, “I marvel, sir, that so good a knight as
you should know his devoir so ill as turn rebel, and give us all this
trouble.”

“I am nun-nun-nun-nun-nun-no knight.”

“What then?”

“A hosier.”

“A what? Then thy armour shall be stripped off, and thou shalt be tied
to a stake in front of the works, and riddled with arrows for a warning
to traitors.”

“N-n-n-n-no! duda-duda-duda-duda-don't do that.”

“Why not?”

“Tuta-tuta-tuta-townsfolk will-h-h-h-hang t'other
buba-buba-buba-buba-bastard.”

“What, whom?”

“Your bub-bub-bub-brother Baldwyn.”

“What, have you knaves ta'en him?”

The warlike hosier nodded.

“Hang the fool!” said Anthony, peevishly.

The warlike hosier watched his eye, and doffing his helmet, took out of
the lining an intercepted letter from the duke, bidding the said Anthony
come to court immediately, as he was to represent the court of Burgundy
at the court of England; was to go over and receive the English king's
sister, and conduct her to her bridegroom, the Earl of Charolois. The
mission was one very soothing to Anthony's pride, and also to his love
of pleasure. For Edward the Fourth held the gayest and most luxurious
court in Europe. The sly hosier saw he longed to be off, and said,
“We'll gega-gega-gega-gega-give ye a thousand angels to raise the
siege.”

“And Baldwyn?”

“I'll gega-gega-gega-gega-go and send him with the money.”

It was now dinner-time; and a flag of truce being hoisted on both sides,
the sham knight and the true one dined together and came to a friendly
understanding.

“But what is your grievance, my good friend?”

“Tuta-tuta-tuta-tuta-too much taxes.”

Denys, on finding the arrow in his right arm, turned his back, which was
protected by a long shield, and walked sulkily into camp. He was met by
the Comte de Jarnac, who had seen his brilliant shot, and finding him
wounded into the bargain, gave him a handful of broad pieces.

“Hast got the better of thy grief, arbalestrier, methinks.”

“My grief, yes; but not my love. As soon as ever I have put down this
rebellion, I go to Holland, and there I shall meet with him.”

This event was nearer than Denys thought. He was relieved from service
next day, and though his wound was no trifle, set out with a stout heart
to rejoin his friend in Holland.

Letters, the color of live coals, had asked their question on the church wall with a blunt, almost household curiosity—why, in such troubled weather of men’s souls, there was no mass for the duke. People who had gone to market for onions and eels found themselves instead standing with necks craned, mouths ajar, staring at scripture written by no human hand. It shone, it wavered, and it thinned like lard in a hot pan, fading slowly until only the lime-washed stones remained and the cold of daylight returned to its proper dominion.

Yet the question lingered as stubbornly as the smell of smoke in a cloak.

The magistrates, not wishing the heavens to outbid them in loyalty, began to buy masses with a generosity that had the clink of coin in it. The curé—an old acquaintance—took this sudden piety in hard cash, and with it indulged a very pretty taste. But miracles, like cheap wine, grow stale if you sip them too long; life moved on, as it always does, from wonder to bargaining.

Denys had begged for his arms.

“Why disgrace him as well as break his heart?” he pleaded, thinking of Gerard.

“Then swear,” came the answer, “on the cross of thy sword thou wilt not leave the bastard’s service until the sedition is put down.”

Need is a hard master. Denys poured out oaths in volleys—thick, quick, and bitter—till they were satisfied. His arms were restored; his liberty, too, in that narrow soldier’s sense which means a man may walk where he is ordered and die where he is paid.

They halted at an inn called The Three Fish, a place that smelled of damp straw, ale-sour boards, and frying fat that had done duty too many days. Marion, catching sight of him, cried out at once, as if she could keep fear at bay by making sport of it:

“I’m out of luck; who would have thought to see you again?”

Then she saw his face was not made for jesting and softened, the way a cook softens a tough scrap with patience and heat.

“What is amiss?”

He told her—of Gerard lost to him in this whirl of politics and steel, and of the promise that had bound him.

Marion’s mind, trained by hard streets and harder reckonings, took a bright view as naturally as it took a quick knife to an apple.

“Gerard is too handsome and too well-behaved to come to harm,” she said, as if those were protections like armour. “Women will always be on his side. Besides, it must go either well or ill with him. If it goes well, he will strike in with good company to Rome; if ill, he will come home again—perhaps there before you, for you have, by all accounts, a trifle of fighting to do in Flanders.”

She fetched the gold pieces he had entrusted to her. He urged her to keep one, then another, as a man presses bread on a hungry child. She refused steadily, with that honest obstinacy that is rarer than piety paid for by corporations. It eased him. It made him think a little better of the world—at least of the corners where a poor little friend walked alone and yet kept her hands clean.

Already the roads were dotted with foot soldiers in twos and threes, trudging lazily toward Flanders. Many were penniless, but bailiffs pushed them on from town to town, and the innkeepers—grumbling, sweating, and making do—were ordered to feed and lodge them. Anthony of Burgundy rode among these stragglers, gathering them as a man gathers loose ears of wheat into his apron, until he entered Flanders with six hundred men under his standard.

On the frontier Baldwyn, his brother, met him with arms, provisions, and more men. Their force was set in order and marched in battle array through several towns, not only unimpeded but acclaimed—shouts in the streets, bells in the air, the whole countryside sounding like a drum of loyalty. The noise of it, hearty and unanimous, sat ill on those who had been told they marched to chastise disaffection.

“This rebellion of ours is a bite,” growled a soldier named Simon, who had elected himself Denys’s comrade.

Denys said nothing. But inside him a vow hardened, like a crust set before the fire: if this rebellion that had cost him Gerard proved no rebellion at all, then, by St. Mars, he would shoot Anthony of Burgundy dead.

That afternoon they saw ahead a town that crouched behind walls thick as old bread and towers like clenched fists. A whisper ran through the ranks—this was a disaffected place. Yet as they approached, the great gate stood open, and each flanking tower showed only a single sentinel, as if the town had nothing to hide and no fear to show. Their formation loosened; men walked easier; harness creaked, and someone even laughed.

Then, when they were within a furlong, the drawbridge over the moat rose slowly, groaning on its chains until it stood upright against the fort. At that very instant the portcullis dropped with an iron rattle, and the walls bristled—lances, crossbows, sudden faces, the neat black mouths of slits alive with intent.

A stern hum rose from the front rank and shivered backward like a plucked string.

“Halt!” Anthony cried. The word ran down the line, and the whole body checked as if it had struck a wall of air.

“Herald to the gate!”

A pursuivant rode out and stopped twenty yards from the gate. He lifted his bugle; the herald’s flag drooped round it, and the summons rang bright, thin, and insolent against the stone. A tall figure in brazen armour appeared over the gate. Fiery words passed—inaudible, but their meaning plain in the way the herald’s shoulders stiffened. He blew one keen note, a threat sharpened by brass, and galloped back with war in his face.

Anthony bent his head to him for the space of two breaths, then wheeled and shouted, “Pioneers, to the van!”

Hedges were levelled; the force took the field and encamped just out of shot. Mounted officers rode south, east, and west to friendly towns for mangonels and palisades, mantelets and raw hides, tar-barrels and carpenters, provisions and all the stubborn furniture of a siege. The camp settled into a new kind of life—mechanical, busy, and incessantly loud: mallets on stakes, saws biting wood, chains clinking, carts rattling, and, above all, the high thin hiss of arrows sewing the air.

At the first clang of the portcullis Denys’s eyes had brightened. When the herald came back with battle in his gaze, Denys saw it and, for the first time in days, cried out, “Courage, tout le monde, le diable est mort.”

If the great warrior whose name he had spoken could have heard, he might have grinned.

The besiegers encamped a furlong from the walls and made roads. Pikemen waited ready for assault; sappers and pioneers crept forward; catapultiers and crossbowmen took their stations. The siege began in the old patient way—filling the moat, mining, breaching, and all the while working under a close rain of quarrels, bolts, stones, and little rocks. A siege was a kind of craft, a trade of wood and rope and leverage, and it demanded a hundred eyes and a mind awake in every limb. To those who watched from safety it might even seem amusing, like a fair; to those beneath the missiles it was a daylong reckoning.

Carpenters advanced behind rolling mantelets to raise a stockade at the very edge of the moat. Some lives were lost—men dropped as suddenly as sacks of meal—but not many, for crossbowmen, Denys among them, rolled up their shields and shot over the workmen’s heads at every besieged who showed so much as a nose, and at every slit or loophole that commanded the ground. Their bolts made a dull, satisfying thunk when they struck wood; a sharper, uglier sound when they found meat.

Under that condensed fire the palisade rose—fresh-cut timber smelling green and raw, sap bleeding where axes had opened it. It stood between the besiegers and the ordinary missiles of the walls.

The defenders answered at night by running out wooden penthouses atop the curtains, fitting beams into square holes built for the purpose. These hoards—true teeth of a medieval fort—gave defenders freer range than any fixed loophole. From them they could drop and shoot with a cruel liberty, as if the wall had grown hands.

The besiegers brought up mangonels and battered those woodworks with huge stones until boards shattered, and the air filled with splinters like flying bones. They built, too, a triangular wooden tower as high as the curtain, kept ready just out of shot, and the sight of it brooding there chilled the town like a bad omen. The defenders began mining beneath the part of the moat where that tower would come, preparing a warm reception. The besiegers mined elsewhere, aiming to get under the square barbican and throw it down.

All this time Denys worked behind his mantelet with another arbalestrier. He made excellent shots—clean, purposeful, the way a cook trims away waste with a sure knife. His skill earned him the peculiar esteem of an unseen archer within the walls, who now and then sent a winged compliment quivering into Denys’s board. One struck within an inch of the narrow slit through which Denys was squinting.

“Peste,” Denys cried, more angry than afraid. “You shoot well, my friend. Come forth and receive my congratulations! Shall merit such as thine hide its head? Comrade, it is one of those cursed Englishmen with his half-ell shaft. I’ll not die till I’ve had a shot at London wall.”

On the defenders’ side a figure soon drew every eye—because he walked where any sensible man would crawl. A tall knight in complete brass paced the battlements under fire, carrying a light but prodigiously long lance with which he directed the defenders’ movements, as if he were conducting music. When disaster befell the besiegers, that knight and that lance were almost always part of it.

Why did not Denys shoot him? Denys did—every day. Other crossbowmen shot. Archers shot. Everybody shot; and the abomination was that he did not mind. Worse: he began to look as if he did not even know when he was hit. Bolts struck and glanced; arrows kissed the metal and fell. He kept pacing, glittering in the bright air, as calmly oblivious as a sailor in wool pacing his deck under harmless rain.

At last the besiegers, spiteful and practical, cursed him and his impervious coat and saved their good steel for softer targets.

The day was bright, clear, not quite frosty. The whole effort concentrated on about two hundred and fifty yards—two curtains and two towers. One tower was the square barbican; another had a pointed roof overlapping on a stone machicolation, so that a row of crenelets grinned between roof and masonry like a mouth of grinders. The curtains wore their hoards, battered by slinging engines.

Along the moat’s edge, on the besiegers’ side, the works sprawled like a gigantic arsenal—longer than broad, peopled by human ants. Levers groaned, winches squealed, pulleys creaked; capstans turned; carts came and went, rattling like bones in a box. Heaps of stone, piles of fascines, stacks of mantelets, rows of fire-barrels sat ready. And through that honest industry flew arrows, back and forth, stitching an invisible cloth. Here and there a man lay flatter than in any decent sleep with feathers stuck in him, and blood oozed darkly into the churned earth.

Opposite the wooden tower, a great penthouse called a “cat” crept toward the curtain, filling the moat with fascines and rubbish pushed out from its mouth. Ropes and pulleys and distant windlasses moved it with slow persistence. The tall knight burned the first cat with blazing tar-barrels. So the besiegers made the roof of this one very steep and covered it with raw hides; the tar slid off, spitting, and did no harm. The knight signalled, and a little trebuchet behind the wall began dropping stones into the moat. At last it found the range, and one stone punched through the cat’s roof, making an ugly wound.

Baldwyn saw, and his temper—always ready as flint—threw sparks. He ordered the great catapult that had been battering the hoards opposite to be turned and levelled, slantwise, at that invulnerable knight.

Denys and his Englishman went to dinner.

For all their murderous attentions, they had made a distant acquaintance, speaking by signs as men do who share a single, constant topic that keeps its importance in peace or war: food. Sometimes Denys would set a piece of bread atop his mantelet; sometimes the archer would dangle something from a string. Thus they dined together as if at the same board—each chewing, each watching, each listening to the battlefield’s rough orchestra: the thump of stones, the twang of bows, the low thunder of shouted orders.

Now the engineers took the unusual step of slinging fifty-pound stones at one man.

The catapult was a beautiful, brutal thing: a fir-tree trunk set to turn on an axis between uprights, not balanced—three-quarters of its length on one side. At the short thick end hung a weight like half a ton, butt toward the enemy. A winch forced the long end down to the earth and pinned it; the weight rose and strained aloft. A stone lay in a sling at the nose. Then the bolt was drawn, and gravity—old and patient—snapped the machine into motion: weight down, long arm up, sling whipping at the top, stone flying with a jerk that seemed to tear the very air.

The huge mass missed the knight but struck the hoard near him, went through roof and floor like paper, and made a gap as wide as a grave. Two things fell out—first the stone, then the mangled body of a besieger it had struck. Down the curtain they went, down, down, and struck the moat almost together. The water closed bubbling on them, swallowing both stone and bone.

“Aha! a good shot,” cried Baldwyn.

The tall knight retired, and the besiegers hooted. He reappeared on the barbican platform, helmet just visible above the parapet, busy as a man in a bakehouse. Soon an enormous Turkish catapult was hauled into place. From that height it flung a twenty-pound stone some two hundred and forty yards; it bounded and knocked dirt into Lord Anthony’s eye and made him swear. The next stone struck a horse drawing a cart of arrows, bowled it dead like a rabbit, and spilled the load.

Then the Turk turned on the besiegers’ wooden tower, supposed to be out of shot. He slung stones cut with sharp edges on purpose and struck it repeatedly, breaking it in several places. Two of the besiegers’ engines were turned on the barbican platform; they rained smaller stones and killed two engineers. But the Turk disdained to answer in kind. He sent a forty-pound stone crashing onto the besiegers’ great catapult near the axis and smashed the whole structure to pieces; the engineers fled, skipping and yelling like boys stung by bees.

In the afternoon Simon, running back to his mantelet from a palisade where he had been shooting, suddenly stared, held out his arms, and rolled face-first into the dirt with an arrow protruding from his back. The Englishman showed himself a moment to enjoy his work. Denys, already prepared, shot; his bolt struck, and the murderous archer staggered away wounded. Simon never moved again.

“I am unlucky in my comrades,” Denys said, and the words tasted like stale ale.

Next morning the besieged saw, with dismay, that the cat was now covered with mattresses and raw hides and was steadily filling the moat. The tall knight stoned it in vain; he flung burning tar-barrels in vain. Then, with his own hands, he lowered by a rope a bag of burning sulphur and pitch. The stench rolled out thick and choking—sulphur’s bitter bite, pitch’s oily reek—so that the men within were smoked like hams.

But Baldwyn, armoured like a lobster in shining plates, ran forward, bounded onto the cat’s roof, and cut the rope. The work went on while smoke curled and thinned, carried away by the indifferent wind.

Then the knight sent fresh engineers into the mine and underpinned the place with beams, smearing them thick with grease and tar, laying a trap in the earth as carefully as a cook lays kindling under a pot.

At break of day the moat was filled. The wooden tower began to move on its wheels toward the curtain where two catapults were already clearing the hoards. Its approach was awful, almost magical, for it moved without visible agency—driven by internal rollers worked by leverage. On its top platform stood the first assailing party, protected in front by the drawbridge of the turret, which stood upright until it would be lowered onto the wall; protected better still by full suits of armour.

The defenders slung stones at the tower and struck it often, but the hides and mattresses drank the blows. Presently it stood at the moat’s edge. The tall knight bade fire the mine beneath it.

At that moment the Turkish engine flung a stone of half a hundredweight right among the knights on the tower. Two were carried off it onto the plain. One lay and writhed; the other neither moved nor spoke.

Now the besieging catapults hurled blazing tar-barrels and set the hoards on both sides aflame. The assailants ran up ladders behind the tower; the drawbridge was lowered onto the battered curtain. In concert the engines fired adjoining works to drive defenders back. Armoured men sprang onto the bridge led by Baldwyn. The invulnerable knight and his men-at-arms met them, and a fearful combat began on that narrow plank of death. Men fell headlong, armour flashing, bodies tumbling like dropped pots.

Fresh besiegers swarmed up behind. The defenders were driven off the bridge. Another minute and the town might have been taken.

But the mine had been timed with a craft as exact as measuring spice: just then the underpinnings gave way. The tower sank suddenly away from the wall, tearing the drawbridge clear and pouring the soldiers off it—against the masonry and into the dry moat below, a heap of iron and limbs.

A fierce shout rose from the defenders. In a moment they surrounded Baldwyn and his fellows—and, strangely, offered quarter. While some disarmed and disposed of the prisoners, others fired the turret in fifty places with a kind of hand-grenades. The tall knight was busiest of all, loading fire-bags onto his long spear and thrusting them into the doomed structure that had lately been so terrible.

To do this he had to stand on a projecting beam of the shattered hoard, holding on by a pikeman’s hand to steady himself.

It provoked Denys. The confusion seemed a cloak. He ran out from behind his mantelet, levelled his crossbow, and shot—missing the knight clean, but driving the bolt into the pikeman’s brain. The hand let go. The tall knight fell heavily from the wall, lance and all.

Denys stared, wonder-struck. In that unlucky moment his arm burned hot, then went cold as if plunged into water. An English arrow had skewered it.

His small pain was swallowed by the larger drama. The knight, armour glittering in the morning sun, fell headlong, but turned as he struck the water and hit with a slap that sounded a mile off. No one thought to see him again. Yet he fell at the edge of the fascines where the turret stood cocked on one side. His spear stuck into them under water; by a mighty effort he worked to the side, but could not climb out.

Anthony sent a dozen knights with a white flag to take him prisoner. The fallen terror submitted like a lamb, saying nothing. They brought him dripping and mud-plastered to Anthony’s tent. At first Anthony laughed at the sight of that once-glittering armour fouled like a pot left too long in ashes. Then his face hardened.

“I marvel, sir,” he said, “that so good a knight as you should know his devoir so ill as turn rebel, and give us all this trouble.”

“I am n-n-n-n-no knight,” the prisoner stammered.

“What then?”

“A hosier.”

“A what? Then thy armour shall be stripped off, and thou shalt be tied to a stake in front of the works, and riddled with arrows for a warning to traitors.”

“N-n-n-no! Duda-duda-don’t do that.”

“Why not?”

“Tuta-tuta-townsfolk will h-h-h-hang t’other buba-buba-bastard.”

“What—whom?”

“Your bub-bub-brother Baldwyn.”

Anthony started as if a hot coal had fallen into his glove. “What, have you knaves ta’en him?”

The warlike hosier nodded.

“Hang the fool!” Anthony said peevishly, more angry at being checked than at the peril.

The hosier watched his eye, then doffed his helmet and drew from its lining a letter—intercepted. It was from the duke, bidding Anthony come to court immediately. He was to represent Burgundy at the court of England; to go over, receive the English king’s sister, and conduct her to her bridegroom, the Earl of Charolois.

The words had the power of perfume: they carried the scent of velvet halls, rich tables, music untroubled by screams, and a court famed as the gayest and most luxurious in Europe. The hosier saw desire rise in Anthony like hunger.

“We’ll gega-gega-give ye a thousand angels,” the hosier stammered, “to raise the siege.”

“And Baldwyn?”

“I’ll gega-gega-go and send him with the money.”

It was dinner-time. A flag of truce was hoisted on both sides. The sham knight and the true one dined together, and by the end of the meal—between bread broken and meat torn—came to a friendly understanding.

“But what is your grievance, my good friend?” Anthony asked, as if rebellion were merely a seasoning that had been overdone.

“Tuta-tuta-too much taxes,” said the hosier, with the plainness of a man who has counted every penny and felt each one taken.

Denys, discovering the arrow in his right arm, turned his back—protected by a long shield—and walked sulkily into camp, the noise of the siege dulled by the rush of blood in his ears. The wound throbbed with its own pulse, like a kettle beginning to simmer.

He met the Comte de Jarnac, who had seen his brilliant shot; finding him wounded into the bargain, the count dropped into his hand a handful of broad pieces, bright as freshly turned loaves.

“Hast got the better of thy grief, arbalestrier, methinks.”

“My grief, yes,” Denys replied, the words tight between his teeth. “But not my love. As soon as ever I have put down this rebellion, I go to Holland; and there I shall meet with him.”

The event was nearer than Denys thought. Next day he was relieved from service; and though his wound was no trifle, he set out with a stout heart to rejoin his friend in Holland, leaving behind him the siege’s clangour and its bitter smoke, and carrying with him the ache of iron in flesh and of a name that tasted, in his mouth, like home bread remembered in exile.
